# 023 · A partitioner written with Math.abs sends one key in two billion to a negative partition

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: counterexample found** | functional | high | cleanup, behaviour change not intended | [`Partitioner#partitionFor`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/kafka/Partitioner.java) | [B11: Property proofs](../../lib/README.md) |

> A custom Kafka partitioner routes a tenant's records by the hash of its id, so that every record of a tenant lands on the same partition. A developer rewrites Kafka's `toPositive(hash) % n`, with its unexplained bit mask, as `Math.abs(hash) % n`, which says what it means. The module's properties file says every hash lands on a partition of the topic. The prover finds the one `int` whose absolute value is negative, and the tool replays it: the partition is negative, which the producer rejects, and that tenant's records are never sent.

## The change

Replace `(hash & 0x7fffffff) % numPartitions` with `Math.abs(hash) % numPartitions`. The mask is there to make the hash positive, and `Math.abs` is the name for that. The tests pass: positive hashes spread as before, and negative hashes land on a partition.

**Before** ([`Partitioner.java`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/kafka/Partitioner.java), line 9):

```java

    private Partitioner() {}

    /** Kafka's {@code Utils.toPositive(hash) % numPartitions}: clear the sign bit, then take the remainder. */
    public static int partitionFor(int hash, int numPartitions) {
        if (numPartitions <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("a topic has at least one partition");
        }
        return (hash & 0x7fffffff) % numPartitions;
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java

    private Partitioner() {}

    /** The hash made positive, modulo the partition count. */
    public static int partitionFor(int hash, int numPartitions) {
        if (numPartitions <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("a topic has at least one partition");
        }
        return Math.abs(hash) % numPartitions;
    }
}
```

<details><summary>Patch</summary>

```diff
--- a/examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/kafka/Partitioner.java
+++ b/examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/kafka/Partitioner.java
@@ -9,11 +9,11 @@ public final class Partitioner {
 
     private Partitioner() {}
 
-    /** Kafka's {@code Utils.toPositive(hash) % numPartitions}: clear the sign bit, then take the remainder. */
+    /** The hash made positive, modulo the partition count. */
     public static int partitionFor(int hash, int numPartitions) {
         if (numPartitions <= 0) {
             throw new IllegalArgumentException("a topic has at least one partition");
         }
-        return (hash & 0x7fffffff) % numPartitions;
+        return Math.abs(hash) % numPartitions;
     }
 }
```

</details>

## What the verifier found

The property `result >= 0 && result < numPartitions` does not hold on every input where `numPartitions > 0` holds. The prover found this input, and the tool replayed it on the method to show what it does:

| Input | The method's outcome |
|---|---|
| `partitionFor(hash=-2147483648, numPartitions=3)` | `-2` |

One input is enough to fail the build. The domain is `hash: int × numPartitions: int`; the search tries small values first so that the witness is readable, and would have covered all of it.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

`Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, because `2^31` does not fit in an `int`. The remainder is then negative, the producer throws `IllegalArgumentException: Invalid partition given with record` on every send for that key, and the tenant whose id hashes to `MIN_VALUE` loses every record, silently if the send is asynchronous and the callback only logs. Nothing else is affected, so dashboards stay green: this is the kind of bug that surfaces as a single customer's complaint months later, with a hash that nobody thinks to check. Kafka's own `Utils.toPositive` has the mask precisely because of this; the Javadoc of `Math.abs` warns about it in its last sentence.

## Why the verdict is right

The property reads: for every `numPartitions > 0`, the result is in `[0, numPartitions)`. JBMC searches small values first and finds nothing, because the bug needs one specific hash out of 2^32. The next pass covers the whole domain and finds it: `hash = -2147483648`. The tool replays the method on that input and reports a negative partition number. A test could have included this value, but only if its author knew the one fact the cleanup forgot; the property states what every partitioner must do, and the prover checks it against every hash.

## What to do

Keep the mask, or use `Math.floorMod(hash, numPartitions)`, which is defined for negative dividends. The property stays in the file, so the next rewrite of this line is checked against every `int` again.

## Evidence

**Provenance:** Constructed from the `Math.abs(x) % n` partitioning bug, which recurs in custom Kafka partitioners and in hash-based sharding generally; Kafka's `Utils.toPositive` exists because of it.

- [Kafka, Utils.toPositive (the mask, with the comment that explains it)](https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/trunk/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/utils/Utils.java)
- [Java API, Math.abs(int): "if the argument is equal to the value of Integer.MIN_VALUE, the result is that same value, which is negative"](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Math.html#abs(int))
